extracted.intended_audience: students/readers of classical Euclidean geometry (learners, teachers, translators)
extracted.subtask_short: dividing geometric figures into equal parts
extracted.subtask_description: Classical Euclidean constructions and definitions showing how to divide polygons (triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, etc.), circles, and solids into equal parts and how to measure surfaces and volumes. Includes constructive methods (diameters, equilateral triangles, equidistant lines) and definitional remarks about solids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a quadrilateral into two equal parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Dividere il quadrilatero in 2 parti uguali (in parti iguales): obtain two equal-area parts of a quadrilateral by drawing appropriate straight lines (through given points, midpoints or using lines equidistant to given lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a line that passes through a given point or midpoint and is equidistant to specified bounding lines; show that if the resulting constituent triangles are equal then the quadrilateral parts are equal. Multiple constructions are given (using diameters, parallels, midpoints, or equidistant lines). The text demonstrates by creating equal triangles and composing/decomposing quadrilaterals accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a quadrilateral using a line through a given interior point
rubrics_metrics.description: If a point inside a quadrilateral is given, one can draw through it a straight line (often equidistant to some given side or line) so that the quadrilateral is divided into two equal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: choose or construct the appropriate equidistant line or use the given point as origin for a line that makes equal triangles on each side; use midpoint constructions of sides or diameters to guarantee equality. The page gives stepwise instructions and diagrammatic references for such constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a quadrilateral by joining midpoints or using opposite angles/diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: You can divide a quadrilateral into equal parts by connecting midpoints or by using lines (diagonals/diameters) related to opposite angles so that resulting triangles or quadrilaterals are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: taking the midpoint of a side and joining to appropriate opposite points, or drawing a diameter/opposite chord that produces equal triangles, then recombining triangles to show equal areas for the two parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct a line that makes two equal triangles (and hence divides a polygon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide a polygon by producing a straight line that creates two triangles equal in area; equality of those triangles implies equality of the polygon parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical approach: create auxiliary points so that the triangles on either side of the dividing line are congruent or have equal base×height, thereby ensuring equal polygonal parts. The text repeatedly reduces polygon division problems to creating equal triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a pentagon (regular) into two equal parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a pentagon equilatero e equiangolo (regular pentagon), divide it into two equal parts by selecting a suitable vertex or point and drawing a straight line to an appropriately constructed point on the opposite side or perimeter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods include: drawing from a chosen vertex a line to a constructed point (e.g., midpoint or intersection determined by auxiliary constructions) so that the resulting subfigures can be shown equal by decomposing into equal triangles and quadrilaterals. The text gives explicit stepwise constructions and special cases (point on side, interior point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a regular pentagon (and other regular n-gons) into multiple equal parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular polygons (pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, etc.) can be divided into 2 or more equal parts by drawing appropriate lines from vertices, midpoints, or by using central constructions that create equal triangles/quadrilaterals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the pentagon the text shows dividing into 2 equal parts; it then generalizes by composing or removing equal triangles/quadrilaterals to divide into more parts. For many-sided regular figures, proceed by choosing vertices/points and repeating the same construction to obtain the desired equal subdivisions (e.g., dividing into 3, 4, ... parts by successive similar operations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a circle into two equal parts (halves)
rubrics_metrics.description: A circle is divided into two equal parts by drawing a diameter through the centre — each semicircle is equal to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the diameter through the given centre (or join given opposite points on the circumference); the resulting semicircles (and corresponding sectors) are equal. The text emphasizes the diameter as the standard way to bisect a circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a circle into three equal parts (trisect the circumference)
rubrics_metrics.description: To divide a circle into three equal arcs, inscribe an equilateral triangle and use its vertices/radii so that the circle's circumference is partitioned into three equal arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: with the centre given, construct an equilateral triangle on the circle (vertices on the circumference) and draw the radii/lines that determine arcs; the three arcs (and corresponding sectors) are equal. The text notes that the chords/radii forming equal central angles yield equal arcs and sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a circle into four equal parts (quartering)
rubrics_metrics.description: A circle is divided into four equal parts by drawing two diameters at right angles (perpendicular diameters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct one diameter, then construct another diameter perpendicular to it through the centre; the four resulting arcs/sectors are equal. The method is described as standard and easy compared to other partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a circle into n equal parts by equally spaced radii/central angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Any circle may be divided into as many equal parts as desired by constructing lines (radii/diameters) that are equally spaced about the centre — i.e., producing equal central angles or equal arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General method: choose a point on the circumference, then step off equal arcs (or use central-angle construction) repeatedly around the circle; radii to those points divide the circle into equal sectors. For certain small n the text gives specific constructions (3 by equilateral triangle, 4 by perpendicular diameters), and for larger n it instructs iterative/proportional constructions or use of equally spaced diameters/lines equidistant about the centre. The page uses the phrase 'linee equediftanti' (equidistant lines) to indicate equally spaced radii/diameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use equal triangles/quadrilaterals to compare/produce equal polygonal areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Many division tasks are reduced to creating pairs of equal triangles (or quadrilaterals) so that combining or removing them shows equality of larger polygonal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual frequently composes and decomposes figures: remove congruent triangles from polygons or attach congruent parts so that equality of remaining figures follows. This is the recurring proof technique: reduce area-equality claims to equality/congruence of constituent triangles or parallelograms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide solids (sphere, cylinder, cone, cube, etc.) by planes/diameters into equal parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Solids may be bisected or partitioned by planes through their centres (or by axes/diameters) so that the resulting solids or surface regions are equal (e.g., a sphere bisected by a plane through the centre yields two hemispheres).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and constructions: the centre and poles of a sphere are defined; planes through the centre divide the sphere into equal portions; lines from the centre to the surface are equal; analogous methods to the circle use diameters and central planes. The text emphasises using symmetry about the centre to guarantee equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure surface area by multiplying linear measures; compute volumes by base area × height
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface area of a rectilinear face is the product of its length and width (area = length × width); a solid's volume is obtained by multiplying the area of its base by its height (the typical prismatic/pyramidal relations and cube-volume as side^3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book explains measurement conventions: to find the area of a face multiply the two orthogonal dimensions; to find the volume of a cube use the third power of the side (cube); to recover a side from a given square area take the square root. Examples and scale factors are remarked ('il quadrato del lato', 'radici'). It also discusses expressing sizes in units (braccia, etc.) and using multiplications and roots in computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming and recognizing solids by faces and bases (definitions used for working/constructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide definitions of solids (piramide, colonna, sfera, cubo) and their characteristic elements (base, faces, centre, poles) to inform constructive and partitioning methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding these definitions is prerequisite to partitioning and measuring: e.g., a pyramid has a base and triangular faces rising to an apex; a column has parallel faces; a sphere has a centre and all radii equal. The text uses these definitions when describing how to divide or measure solids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a circle (or sector) into parts with equal measured area via proportional constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: To divide a circular region into parts that are equal in area or in proportion, use chords, diameters, or radii positioned so that the enclosed sectors/figures have the desired quantitative proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains that equal central angles (or equal radii separation) produce equal arcs and thus equal sectors. For proportional divisions (not necessarily equal), one can use constructions based on locating points such that the arc lengths or associated chord/radius combinations produce the required areas; several worked examples and remarks on practicality (difficulty for fine subdivisions) are given.
